questions.prompt: What is the correct, precise definition of 'authorization' as distinct from 'authentication'?
options: Authorization is the process of proving who a user is
Authorization determines what an already-authenticated user is allowed to do
Authorization is another name for Single Sign-On
Authorization is a synonym for Multi-Factor Authentication
questions.explain: Authentication answers 'who are you?'. Authorization is the separate, subsequent step that determines what an authenticated user is permitted to do, via profiles, permission sets, role hierarchy, and sharing.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A describes authentication, not authorization — proving identity is a completely separate step that happens first. Authorization only begins once identity has already been established.

questions.prompt: An employee clicks a tile on their company's Okta dashboard and lands directly in Salesforce, already authenticated, with no redirect initiated by Salesforce. What SSO pattern is this, and which party started the flow?
options: SP-initiated SSO; the flow started at Salesforce
IdP-initiated SSO; the flow started at the identity provider's own portal
Delegated authentication; the flow started at a client-hosted web service
Just-in-Time provisioning; the flow started at the SAML assertion
questions.explain: Because the user started at Okta's own portal and Okta proactively sent a signed assertion to Salesforce, this is IdP-initiated SSO.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: SAML stands for Security Assertion Markup ________.
questions.explain: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) is an XML-based open standard for exchanging authentication and authorization data between an identity provider and a service provider.

questions.prompt: Match each identity protocol to the primary signed artifact it produces.
right: An access token authorizing API calls
An ID token (a JWT) proving who the user is
A signed XML assertion vouching for authentication
questions.explain: SAML produces a signed XML assertion. Plain OAuth produces an access token for authorizing resource access. OpenID Connect layers identity on top of OAuth by additionally issuing a JWT-formatted ID token.

questions.prompt: Select every OAuth 2.0 flow that is appropriate for unattended, server-to-server integrations with no user present.
options: JWT Bearer flow
Client Credentials flow
User-Agent (Implicit) flow
Web Server (Authorization Code) flow requiring interactive browser consent
questions.explain: JWT Bearer and Client Credentials are both designed for unattended, machine-to-machine authentication with no user present. The Implicit flow and interactive Authorization Code flow both assume a user is present in a browser to grant consent.

questions.prompt: A developer accidentally commits a Connected App's Consumer Secret to a public source code repository. What is the most accurate description of the resulting risk?
options: There is no real risk, since the Consumer Secret is a public value like the Consumer Key
An attacker can now potentially impersonate the connected app itself in OAuth flows that rely on that secret, such as Client Credentials or Web Server flows
The risk is limited to that one developer's personal Salesforce login
The Consumer Secret automatically expires after 24 hours, so the leak is self-limiting
questions.explain: The Consumer Secret must be protected like a password — a leak lets an attacker impersonate the entire connected app for any flow relying on it, which is a materially more dangerous exposure than a single leaked user password.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the SAML Web Browser SSO POST flow (SP-initiated) in the correct order.
items: Salesforce detects the user is unauthenticated and redirects the browser to the IdP
The IdP returns a signed SAML assertion inside an auto-submitting HTML form
The browser POSTs the form to the SP's Assertion Consumer Service URL
Salesforce validates the assertion's signature and establishes a session
questions.explain: SP-initiated SAML SSO begins with Salesforce redirecting the unauthenticated user to the IdP, which authenticates them and returns a signed assertion via an auto-submitting form; the browser then POSTs it to the ACS URL, where Salesforce validates it and logs the user in.

questions.prompt: A client's mobile app needs to both call the Salesforce REST API on a user's behalf AND display that user's name and email after they sign in with Google. Which OAuth/OIDC detail is most relevant to making the second part work?
options: Requesting the `openid` scope so an ID token carrying identity claims is issued alongside the access token
Using the Username-Password flow instead of any redirect-based flow
Disabling all OAuth scopes except `full`
Switching from OAuth to delegated authentication
questions.explain: An access token alone only authorizes API calls — it doesn't reliably carry identity claims. Requesting the `openid` scope triggers issuance of an ID token (a JWT) that carries claims like name and email.

questions.prompt: What does enabling My Domain give a Salesforce org?
options: A unique, org-specific subdomain that serves as the foundation for SSO, Identity Provider, and Auth. Provider configuration
A free upgrade to unlimited API calls
Automatic enrollment in Multi-Factor Authentication
A duplicate sandbox environment
questions.explain: My Domain gives an org a unique, stable subdomain (e.g., yourcompany.my.salesforce.com) that nearly every identity feature in this course — SSO, Identity Provider, Auth. Providers — depends on as its anchor.
questions.distractorExplain: My Domain has no effect on API call limits — option B confuses a login/branding feature with a licensing or governor-limit concept, which My Domain simply does not touch.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the user field used to match an incoming SAML assertion's Subject to an existing Salesforce user record is called the ________.
questions.explain: The Federation ID (FederationIdentifier field) is the shared identifier both the IdP and SP agree represents the same person, used to link identities without exposing any login credential.

questions.prompt: A client wants custom logic to assign a Salesforce profile based on a 'department' attribute carried in the SAML assertion, every time a new user is Just-in-Time provisioned. What should the architect implement?
options: A class implementing the Auth.SamlJitHandler interface, registered in the SAML JIT Handler field on the SAML Single Sign-On Setting
A Flow triggered by the login history object
A custom report filtered on department
A modification to the user's Federation ID field
questions.explain: Custom SAML JIT provisioning logic, like deriving a profile from an assertion attribute, is implemented via a class implementing Auth.SamlJitHandler, registered as the org's SAML JIT Handler.

questions.prompt: Select every verification method that satisfies Salesforce's Multi-Factor Authentication requirement as a strong, currently-recommended second factor.
options: Salesforce Authenticator push approval
A WebAuthn/U2F hardware security key
A third-party TOTP authenticator app
Relying on the user's IP address alone
questions.explain: Salesforce Authenticator, hardware security keys, and TOTP authenticator apps are all legitimate MFA second factors. An IP address alone is not a second authentication factor at all.

questions.prompt: Match each Setup page to what it configures.
right: Trusting an external IdP's certificate so Salesforce can act as an SP
Enabling Salesforce to sign and issue assertions to downstream service providers
Configuring trust in an external OIDC or social sign-on issuer
questions.explain: Single Sign-On Settings configures Salesforce as an SP trusting an external IdP. Identity Provider enables Salesforce to act as an IdP. Auth. Providers configures trust in external OIDC/social issuers. My Domain registers the org's unique subdomain, a prerequisite for the other three.

questions.prompt: An admin successfully tests SP-initiated SSO using their own admin account, then immediately disables the standard Salesforce login page for every profile in the org, including System Administrator. What is the main risk?
options: There is no risk; a successful test with an admin account proves the configuration is safe for everyone
If the external IdP later has an outage or misconfiguration, there is no break-glass path left for anyone, including that same admin, to get back in
The risk only affects non-admin users, never admins
SSO configurations cannot actually be disabled once enabled, so this scenario is impossible
questions.explain: Disabling standard login for all profiles, including admins, removes any break-glass path. A single successful test doesn't verify recovery behavior during a future IdP outage — the standard mitigation is to keep at least one admin profile able to use standard login.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of registering and rolling out a My Domain subdomain in the correct order.
items: Enter a subdomain name and click Check Availability
Click Register Domain and wait for provisioning
Test the new domain thoroughly before wider rollout
questions.explain: My Domain rollout starts with checking name availability, then registering and waiting for provisioning, then thoroughly testing the new domain, and only then deploying it to all users — since deployment changes the org's live login URL for everyone.

questions.prompt: A company has ten applications and wants every pair of them to support direct SSO with each other without a central identity hub. What is the main architectural problem with this point-to-point approach as the company keeps adding applications?
options: Point-to-point trust relationships grow combinatorially as applications are added, and there's no single place to centrally enforce MFA or deactivation
Point-to-point trust is actually more secure than any hub-and-spoke model in every case
SAML cannot technically support more than two trust relationships at once
This approach eliminates the need for any authentication protocol at all
questions.explain: As applications are added, the number of pairwise trust relationships needed grows much faster than the number of apps, and enforcement of policies like MFA and deactivation has to be replicated everywhere instead of centralized in one hub.

questions.prompt: A consumer electronics company wants a public site where anyone can self-register to track a warranty claim, and separately wants verified repair-shop partners to have ongoing, role-based access across multiple customers' claims. Why should these two populations receive different identity treatment?
options: They shouldn't; every external user should be treated identically regardless of relationship type

Consumers are a CIAM population prioritizing low-friction self-registration, while partners need bounded, admin-approved onboarding with delegated administration and sharing that spans multiple customer Accounts
Repair-shop partners should always self-register exactly like consumers do
Consumers always need broader data access than partners
questions.explain: Consumers and partners have opposing design priorities — low-friction self-service versus bounded, role-based, admin-approved access spanning multiple Accounts — and conflating the two produces a poor fit for at least one group.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an Experience Cloud user's data visibility is typically scoped by their link to a ________ record, which in turn ties to an Account.
questions.explain: An Experience Cloud user's identity is almost always tied to a Contact record, and through that Contact, to an Account — this Contact/Account linkage is what drives sharing-based visibility into records like cases and orders.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about delegated authentication, as compared to SAML/OIDC federation.
options: The user's actual password passes through Salesforce's login form on its way to the client-hosted authentication endpoint
It requires the client to build and indefinitely maintain their own authentication web service
Salesforce never sees the user's password at any point, exactly like SAML
It naturally supports modern MFA and social sign-on flows just as well as federation does
questions.explain: Delegated authentication sends the raw password through Salesforce's login form to a client-hosted callout, unlike federation where Salesforce never sees the password. It also requires the client to build and maintain a custom endpoint indefinitely, and it doesn't naturally support modern MFA or social login flows the way federation does.

questions.prompt: An external expense-reporting API needs to know exactly which individual Salesforce user submitted each callout, to drive its own per-employee approval routing. Which Named Credential identity type should be used, and why?
options: Named Principal, because it's simpler to configure
Per-User, because each user authenticates individually with the external system, preserving per-user accountability the external system needs
Neither; Named Credentials cannot be used for this scenario
Named Principal, because all Salesforce users should appear identical to external systems
questions.explain: Per-User authentication lets each Salesforce user authenticate individually with the external system, preserving the per-user accountability the expense API's approval routing depends on. Named Principal would collapse everyone into one shared identity, breaking that routing.

questions.prompt: Match each session/token concept to its definition.
right: How long a session stays valid without activity before requiring re-authentication
A long-lived credential used to obtain new access tokens without re-prompting the user
Standard vs. High Assurance classification of a session based on how it was authenticated
Increasing a session's security level mid-session, without a full re-login
questions.explain: Session timeout governs inactivity expiration. Session Security Level classifies a session as Standard or High Assurance. Step-up authentication raises that level mid-session. Refresh tokens are the long-lived credential used to mint new access tokens.

questions.prompt: What is the core mechanical difference between federated authentication (SAML/OIDC) and delegated authentication?
options: Federation relies on signed assertions/tokens so the SP never sees the password; delegated authentication sends the raw password to a client-hosted callout
There is no real difference; they are two names for the same mechanism
Delegated authentication is newer and more modern than SAML or OIDC
Federation requires a password to be emailed to the SP administrator
questions.explain: Federation protocols never expose the password to the relying party — only a signed artifact crosses the boundary. Delegated authentication, by contrast, has the password itself travel through Salesforce's login form to a client-hosted validation endpoint.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the current (non-Legacy) Named Credential schema, the object that holds the actual authentication protocol and the Named Principal/Per-User identity type is called the ________.
questions.explain: The current schema splits the Named Credential (endpoint/callout settings) from the External Credential, which holds the authentication protocol and identity type, allowing it to be reused across multiple Named Credentials.

questions.prompt: In the workforce case study, the client's corporate directory (Entra ID, fed by Workday) should already handle MFA and SSO for most apps. What role should Salesforce play, and what provisioning gap must still be addressed beyond JIT?
options: Salesforce should be the IdP, and JIT alone is fully sufficient for the whole user lifecycle
Salesforce should be the SP, and JIT alone is insufficient because it can't handle deactivation or pre-provisioning before a user's first login
Salesforce should be neither IdP nor SP, since SSO is impossible with Entra ID
Salesforce should be the IdP, and delegated authentication should replace SAML entirely
questions.explain: With an existing enterprise hub (Entra ID) as the authoritative identity source, Salesforce should be the SP. JIT only fires at login, so it can't deactivate a terminated employee who never logs in again — a SCIM-style or connector-based provisioning approach is needed to close that gap.

questions.prompt: In the customer portal case study, marketing wants minimal signup friction while support wants confidence that a user is who they claim to be before showing order history. Which pattern resolves this tension?
options: Requiring full identity verification at the moment of initial signup for every visitor
Progressive profiling — minimal friction at signup, with stronger identity checks required only when sensitive data or actions are requested
Removing all authentication requirements from the portal entirely
Using delegated authentication instead of self-registration
questions.explain: Progressive profiling lets signup stay low-friction while deferring stronger identity confidence checks to the specific moment they're actually needed, such as viewing sensitive order history.

questions.prompt: Select every pair that correctly represents one of the recurring identity design trade-off axes discussed in this course.
options: Friction vs. identity confidence
Centralization vs. autonomy
Named Principal simplicity vs. Per-User accountability
SAML vs. OIDC is always a trade-off with no correct default
questions.explain: Friction vs. identity confidence, centralization vs. autonomy, and Named Principal simplicity vs. Per-User accountability are all named trade-off axes. SAML vs. OIDC is not framed as an open-ended trade-off in this course — the protocol choice is typically driven by what the existing infrastructure actually supports.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: recognizing that a generally-true rule doesn't apply because a scenario's specific details make it inapplicable is called avoiding the ________ trap.
questions.explain: Exam-style scenario traps typically come from over-generalizing a rule that's often true ('prefer modern protocols', 'Salesforce is usually the SP') into a universal rule, without checking the scenario's specific constraints.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a practical identity security review in the recommended order.
items: Confirm My Domain and Single Sign-On Settings fundamentals are configured as expected
Audit Connected Apps for OAuth scope minimization and Permitted Users policies
Check Session Settings and Session Security Levels
Spot-check a sample of user records for Federation ID consistency
Interview the client's team about their actual offboarding process
questions.explain: A practical review starts with the identity fundamentals (My Domain, SSO Settings), moves to Connected App scope/policy auditing, then session security configuration, then data-level spot checks, and finishes by verifying real-world process against documentation — since that's where most practical gaps are actually found.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an identity architecture that contains damage from an outage, leak, or mistake, rather than preventing all failure outright, is said to ________.
questions.explain: Failing safely means a break-glass path survives an IdP outage, a leaked token's damage is limited by minimal scope, and similar properties — containment of failure's impact, not its total absence.

questions.prompt: Match each exam-style scenario trap to the correct underlying identity concept it tests.
left: A client's AD FS deployment has never been updated to support OpenID Connect, but still needs SSO into Salesforce
Employees should be able to SSO from inside Salesforce into a separate internal expense tool
An admin tests SSO successfully once, then disables standard login for every profile
A client enables SAML JIT provisioning and considers it sufficient for full user lifecycle management
right: Provisioning gap: JIT only covers creation/update at login, not deactivation
Protocol choice must match what the existing infrastructure actually supports, not just the generally 'more modern' option
Lockout risk: no break-glass path survives if the IdP later fails
IdP vs. SP role: Salesforce must be the IdP when another app relies on a Salesforce login
questions.explain: Each trap tests a specific concept: matching the protocol to existing infrastructure, correctly identifying which party is the IdP, recognizing the lockout risk of disabling standard login too early, and recognizing that JIT alone doesn't cover the full user lifecycle.
